transcript.text: LG F4V5VYP0W says OE and the clothes are sat in water. I'm not opening the little door at the bottom because last time I did that it flooded the whole kitchen. What else can I do?

The OE code on LG machines means 'Error Outlet' – the machine has tried to drain but couldn't empty within about 13 minutes. Given your fear of flooding from the filter, checking the hose is a much safer first step. Please pull the machine away from the wall just enough to see the back. Check if the drain hose is kinked or crushed. Also, check where it goes into the standpipe or sink waste; if the hose is pushed in too far (more than 15cm), it can create a blockage. If the hose looks clear and not pushed in too deep, try lifting the end of the hose and holding it over a bucket or sink for a minute. Does water flow out freely? If you see no water coming out, the blockage is likely further down (in the household plumbing) or the pump isn't working. If water does come out but slowly, the filter might be partially blocked. Let me know what you find with the hose first.
Ok, the machine was pushed right back against the wall and the hose was squashed behind it. I've pulled it out and straightened it. Do I need to try a spin again now?

Yes, you can try that now. Since the hose was squashed against the wall, that kink likely prevented the machine from draining, which triggered the OE code and stopped the spin cycle (LG machines won't spin if there is still water in the drum). Straightening the hose should have fixed it. Please run a drain or spin-only programme to see if it empties properly now. If it drains successfully, you can just restart your wash as normal. If it stops again with the OE code despite the hose being clear, we will need to check the filter next.
I tried the spin again. It drained a little slower than normal and then showed OE again. The water's still in the drum.

Before you start, switch it off and unplug it. The fact that it drained 'a little slower than normal' before failing again suggests there is a partial blockage preventing the pump from working efficiently. This is most commonly caused by debris caught in the pump filter or on the small plastic impeller (the fan-like part) inside the filter housing. I understand your concern about flooding, but we need to clear this obstruction for the machine to work. To keep it safe and contained: place a shallow tray or large baking tin directly in front of the filter door, and stack several thick towels inside and around it. Then carefully open the flap and unscrew the filter slowly — let any water drip into the tray/towels rather than onto the floor. Once you have the filter out, could you tell me if there was a blockage (like coins or lint) in it, and whether the small plastic impeller inside the hole turns freely by hand?
No, I'm not unscrewing the filter, that's what flooded my kitchen last time. I do have towels and a baking tray though, so is there a safer way to get the water out?

Yes, there is a much safer way to remove the water without touching the filter. Please take the end of the drain hose (the one at the back) and lower it into your baking tray or a large bucket on the floor. Gravity will pull the water out through the hose. Once it has drained, try running a spin cycle again to see if the machine can complete the job with the hose clear.
Ok, I can try that with the hose into the baking tray. Will it flood though? The tray's quite small and I've got laminate floor. Is there a way to do it that won't spill everywhere?

A small tray is most likely not safe for that much water, especially on laminate which can warp if it seeps underneath. To avoid a mess entirely, use a large bucket or your kitchen sink instead. Lower the end of the drain hose into the bucket/sink and let gravity pull the water out slowly—this takes a bit longer but won't spill anywhere. Once the drum is empty, try running a spin cycle again to see if it completes successfully.

The sink's a bit awkward as the machine's on the floor. Isn't there the small tube behind the little door at the bottom that you drain it through? I'd be ok using that with the towels and tray, as long as I'm not touching the filter itself.

Before you start, switch it off and unplug it. Yes, that small tube is indeed an emergency drain hose (often hidden behind a flap or just accessible at the bottom). It allows you to remove the water without opening the main filter. To do this safely: place your baking tray and towels on the floor directly below it. Pull the cap off the end of the thin black tube, let the water flow into the tray or bucket, and replace the cap once empty. Does the water come out freely from this tube?
Ok, I've got the towels and tray down and I'm opening just the small tube, not the filter. It's draining, but I'll need to empty the tray a few times. What do I do after that?

Run a 'Drain' or 'Spin Only' programme and listen carefully: can you hear the pump humming or buzzing from behind that bottom flap while it tries to drain? If you hear it working hard but no water comes out (or very little), there is likely something stuck in the impeller inside the filter housing. If it is silent, the pump motor itself may have failed.
Ok, the tray's emptied and the drum is empty now. I ran the spin and the pump hums, with an occasional rattle, but it still shows OE. I'm still not opening the filter.

Since the drum is now empty but the machine still shows OE and makes a rattling hum when trying to drain, it suggests that something is physically blocking the pump's internal fan (impeller) or the pump itself has failed. Because you are not comfortable opening the filter housing to clear this blockage yourself, you will need an engineer to open the appliance and check the pump and internal hoses for debris.
